title: Your Kids Can Learn 10x Less in 10x Less Time
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer responds to the claim, popular among tech-adjacent parents, that school is too slow and that software can help kids learn many times faster, by asking the question such claims skip: learn what? He grounds the argument in a fifth-grade math lesson where a class spent twenty minutes on two multiplication problems a calculator could solve instantly. Meyer itemizes what students were actually doing in that time: connecting area models to the standard algorithm, estimating first, deepening place value understanding, and learning to negotiate ideas with classmates. His move is to reframe speed claims as goal reduction, arguing that accelerated models often save time by quietly dropping conceptual depth and the social goal of learning with diverse peers. The second half checks in on Alpha School, noting that its public Unbound Academy promised 60% math proficiency and delivered 10%, that its leadership distances itself from a school its employees govern, and that its private schools appear academically selective. The call is close because the Alpha School section is ed-tech critique, but the lead essay is a pedagogy argument about conceptual depth, so it sits in Learning & Curriculum.
points: Meyer's rebuttal to '10x faster' learning claims is that speed usually comes from committing to fewer goals, such as shallower math or learning alongside fewer, less different peers.
Twenty minutes on two problems let fifth graders connect area models to the standard algorithm, preventing the belief that 'math is magic.'
Partial products and area models expose place value (a 4 that is actually 200 times larger than a 2) that the standard algorithm conceals.
Alpha School's public Unbound Academy promised 60% math proficiency and delivered 10%, while its founders and employees sat on the school's board.
Meyer notes Unbound runs about four hours of daily app time and that Alpha's private freshmen post SAT scores 38% above the Texas average despite claims of non-selective admissions.
quotes: I build curriculum and technology for schools, so I too experience a shiver at the thought of kids learning more, better, or faster. But I am also working weekly in a public fifth-grade math classroom this year, which helps me understand that the right follow-up question whenever anyone claims they can help kids learn 2x, 5x, or 10x faster is “learn what?

They were developing conceptual connections. They solved the same problems in three different ways, connecting older methods like area models and newer methods like the standard algorithm. Without those connections, many kids would inadvertently learn ideas like math is magic.
They were developing their understanding of place value. 4 isn’t two times as large as 2 in the problem above as it seems to many students. It’s 200 times larger.

The public can debate those goals, of course, but they require resources, chief among them time. Doing more stuff generally requires more time. One weird trick for saving time, more and more parents are learning, is to commit to fewer goals.

I’m never going to be content with the work we do in schools, but I will always be impressed by the teachers, schools, and parents who commit every day to meeting ambitious goals with what few resources they have, to do more with less, unbothered by people who believe it is a great accomplishment to do less with less.
Unbound Academy is non-selective and tuition-free. The schools Liemandt goes on to discuss are selective and fee-based, which are crucial differences.
None of those people have answered to Arizona taxpayers for promising 60% math proficiency and delivering 10%.
My interest in Alpha School is pretty tight: Is there anything here for kids outside the top tax bracket? Can 99% of schools learn anything from Alpha School?
